summary: Describes a Same-Origin Policy requirement for RPKI Repository Delta Protocol servers and clients. Applying it to client and server communication isolates delta and snapshot files from different repository servers, which reduces possible attack vectors. It updates RFC 8182.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule says a helper may only fetch files from the place it was told to visit, not from some other stranger's place. That prevents mix-ups and tricks.

questions: how to secure rpki repository delta protocol
what is the rrdp same-origin policy
why does rrdp need a same-origin policy
subtitle: RRDP servers and clients must keep snapshot and delta fetches on the same origin as the update notification file.

tldr.problem: The original RRDP specification did not forbid cross-origin URIs in the Update Notification file and was silent on HTTP redirects, so one repository server could make clients load files from another and raise resource use.
tldr.mechanism: Servers and relying parties must apply a Same-Origin Policy: referenced URIs and HTTP redirects must keep the same scheme, host and port as the Update Notification file.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 8182. A relying party that detects a violation rejects the file or session, so RRDP cannot be used for it.

today: RFC 9674 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024. It updates RFC 8182 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Cross-Origin Problem
sections.content:
A Same-Origin Policy (SOP) restricts how a document loaded from one origin can interact with resources from another; RFC 6454 gives the concept of an origin. The first RRDP specification, RFC 8182, did not explicitly disallow cross-origin URI references from the Update Notification file to Delta and Snapshot files, and it was silent on HTTP redirection.

As a result, one Repository Server can reference RRDP resources on another and inappropriately raise resource consumption for both RRDP clients and the referenced server. An adversary could use cross-origin HTTP redirects for similar effects.
sections.plainLanguage: Without the rule, one shop could send everybody's helpers to another shop and swamp it.

sections.title: Rules for Repository Servers
sections.content:
Repository Servers and clients MUST apply a Same-Origin Policy to both the URIs in an Update Notification file and any HTTP redirects. Two items are added to the checklist in Section 3.5.1.3 of RFC 8182.

  • The uri attribute in the snapshot element and optional delta elements MUST have the same scheme, host and port as the URI of the Update Notification file.
  • The server MUST NOT respond with HTTP redirects to a location with a different origin.
sections.plainLanguage: The shop may only point to its own shelves and may not send customers to another street.

sections.title: Rules for Relying Parties
sections.content:
A relying party MUST verify that the uri attributes in the Update Notification file have the same origin as the file itself. If this fails, the file MUST be rejected and RRDP cannot be used. Implementations SHOULD log a message when cross-origin referrals are detected.

It MUST NOT follow HTTP redirection when downloading Update Notification, Delta and Snapshot files if the target origin differs from that of the Update Notification file. If this fails, the RRDP session MUST be rejected and RRDP cannot be used, and implementations SHOULD log it.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper checks every address, refuses to go to the wrong shop, and writes a note when it sees one.

sections.title: Deployability and Security
sections.content:
The RFC reports that, in rpkiviews archives from April to September 2024, only one RRDP server reached from the five RIR Trust Anchor Locators used a same-origin HTTP redirect. From October 2021 to October 2024 no servers were observed using cross-origin URIs in Update Notification files. So the requirement does not make commonly used operations non-compliant.

The security point is that cross-origin requests let one repository operator raise resource consumption for other operators and RRDP clients. The RFC says a future RRDP version could instead use relative URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost nobody was doing the bad thing, so the new rule breaks almost nothing.
